name: CryptPad
purpose: End-to-end encrypted collaborative office suite — documents, spreadsheets, kanban, forms, polls — where the server stores only ciphertext and encryption keys travel in the URL fragment.
journalism_use_case: Collaborative drafting and shared notes on a sensitive investigation where the hosting provider must not be able to read the material — replacing Google Docs for the planning document, the source list and the draft, which is where newsrooms most often leak their own investigations to a third party.
pros: Zero-knowledge server design means the operator — including you, if self-hosted — cannot read documents, which is a structural answer to the Google Docs problem rather than a policy promise
Covers the formats a newsroom actually collaborates in (documents, sheets, kanban, forms), so it can genuinely replace a cloud suite for sensitive work rather than only for text
AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable, very actively maintained (2026.10.1 released 2026-11-10; pushed 2026-11-16) with a substantial community (8,087 stars)
Link-based access with no account requirement makes it usable by an external collaborator or source without onboarding
cons: Keys in the URL fragment means link handling IS key handling: a link pasted into Slack, email or a chat log hands over the document, and this is the dominant real-world failure mode
372 open issues and a complex browser-side cryptographic application, so the attack surface is the browser and any compromise there defeats the encryption
Performance and feature depth are below commercial office suites, which creates pressure to revert to Google Docs for convenience — a social problem that will decide whether adoption sticks
Self-hosting requires real operations care, and a misconfigured instance (or a compromised server serving modified JavaScript) can undermine the encryption model entirely
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 8,087 stars with 372 open issues, release 2026.10.1 (2026-11-10), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0. CryptPad's zero-knowledge model is documented by the project and it operates a public instance; the key-in-URL design is inherent and openly documented.
assessment: Adopt it for sensitive collaborative work and self-host it, with one rule drilled into the team: the link is the key, so links go only through a channel you would send the document itself through. For your profile this replaces the single most common and least-discussed leak in investigative work — the shared planning document on a third-party cloud. Expect to actively defend adoption against the convenience of commercial suites; that is the real implementation challenge, not the deployment.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 2026.10.1 (2026-11-10), 8,087 stars, 372 open issues. Frequent dated releases under a commercial sponsor (XWiki SAS) with public-instance operation.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered to users obliges source publication. Running the released version for your newsroom carries no obligation.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: a single VM with modest resources serves a small newsroom; storage grows with document history. Operating effort is moderate — it is a web application with a cryptographic front end, so updates matter. The public CryptPad instance has free and paid tiers whose prices were not verified here.
privacy: The server stores only ciphertext, so a hosting compromise or legal demand yields nothing readable — the strongest property available for collaborative documents. The two residual risks are link disclosure (keys in URLs) and browser compromise, both of which are user-side and must be addressed by practice rather than configuration.
alternatives: Nextcloud with server-side or end-to-end encryption for a broader self-hosted suite with weaker confidentiality
Etherpad self-hosted for simple shared text without encryption
Local files plus encrypted transfer for the most sensitive documents, accepting the collaboration cost
blockers: Document keys travel in URLs — link handling is key handling

name: Nextcloud
purpose: Self-hosted file-sync, sharing and collaboration platform with an app ecosystem covering documents, calendars, chat, forms and workflow, plus server-side and optional end-to-end encryption.
journalism_use_case: The practical replacement for commercial cloud storage in a newsroom that must keep documents on its own infrastructure: file sync for reporters, controlled external sharing with partners, and an app ecosystem that covers the ordinary office needs that would otherwise push people back to Google Drive.
pros: Breadth is the reason it works socially: file sync, sharing, calendars and collaborative editing in one self-hosted platform means reporters have fewer reasons to use a commercial alternative
Mature external-sharing controls (password-protected links, expiry, upload-only shares) make partner collaboration manageable without handing documents to a third party
AGPL-3.0 with an enormous community (37,542 stars) and a very active release cadence (v33.0.11, 2026-11-12; pushed 2026-11-17), plus a commercial support option for newsrooms that need it
Self-hosted means full control over location, retention and backups — which for an exile outlet can also mean choosing a jurisdiction deliberately
cons: Server-side encryption protects against disk theft, not against the server operator or a server compromise — so unlike CryptPad, Nextcloud's default model does not protect documents from whoever controls the host, and the optional end-to-end encryption app has historically been limited in scope and maturity

3,948 open issues, the largest in the catalogue, reflecting a very large application surface — operating it well means staying on top of updates, and a neglected Nextcloud is a serious liability holding your documents
Operational burden is real: PHP application, database, background jobs, storage and regular upgrades, with a history of upgrade friction between major versions
Release-object and tag divergence (v33.0.11 release against a v35.0.3 tag) means version tracking needs care
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 37,542 stars with 3,948 open issues, release v33.0.11 (2026-11-12), tag v35.0.3, pushed 2026-11-17, AGPL-3.0. The scale of adoption is clear from the metrics; the limitations of server-side encryption are documented by the project itself.
assessment: Adopt it as the newsroom's general document infrastructure, and be precise about what it protects against: Nextcloud keeps your documents out of a commercial cloud and under your jurisdiction, which is valuable, but it does not make them unreadable to whoever holds the server. Put genuinely sensitive material in CryptPad or encrypted containers, and use Nextcloud for the everyday. Budget permanent administrator attention — the open-issue count is a fair warning about surface area.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v33.0.11 (2026-11-12), tag v35.0.3, 37,542 stars, 3,948 open issues. Very frequent releases with commercial backing; the enormous backlog reflects application breadth and a large user base.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Some enterprise-oriented apps and integrations have separate commercial terms.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered to users obliges source publication. Nextcloud GmbH also sells enterprise subscriptions with support and some additional components — a commercial relationship, not a licence restriction on the server.
costs: No software fee for the community server. Infrastructure estimate: one VM with a database for a small newsroom, scaling with storage — the cost is storage plus permanent administrator time, which is the dominant item. Nextcloud GmbH enterprise subscriptions are priced per user (not verified in this survey). Assumptions: self-hosted, small team, moderate storage.
privacy: Self-hosting gives you control of location, retention and access. The important limitation: server-side encryption does not protect against the operator or a compromised server, so Nextcloud is a jurisdiction-and-control improvement over commercial cloud rather than a confidentiality guarantee. Treat the server as able to read everything on it.
alternatives: CryptPad for documents that must be unreadable to the server
Syncthing for peer-to-peer file sync with no server at all
Commercial cloud storage — the thing this replaces; avoid for source material
blockers: Server-side encryption does not protect documents from the server operator or a host compromise

name: Tor Browser Launcher
purpose: Linux helper that downloads, verifies the signature of, installs and launches Tor Browser, keeping it updated and integrating it into the desktop.
journalism_use_case: Getting Tor Browser onto reporters' Linux machines with signature verification done correctly — because the step people skip is verification, and an unverified Tor Browser download is precisely the attack a hostile network operator would mount against a journalist.
pros: Automates GPG signature verification, which is the security-critical step that manual downloaders omit — this is the tool's real contribution
Keeps Tor Browser updated, and an outdated Tor Browser is a meaningful risk given that browser exploits are the standard route to deanonymisation
MIT licensed and now maintained under the Tor Project organisation (transfer from micahflee verified by redirect in this session), which is a governance improvement
Packaged in major Linux distributions, so installation is usually a single package-manager command
cons: Release metadata is stale (v0.3.7 from 2024-01-28 against tag v0.3.9), so the published release lags the tag line and version tracking is awkward for a security tool
89 open issues against 890 stars, and the launcher is a thin wrapper whose own bugs can block updates — an ironic failure mode for an updater
Linux only; Windows and macOS users download Tor Browser directly and must verify manually, so this solves the problem for only part of a mixed team
Using Tor at all can be conspicuous on a monitored network, which the launcher does nothing to address — bridges must be configured separately
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 890 stars with 89 open issues, release v0.3.7 (2024-01-28), tag v0.3.9, pushed 2026-11-05, MIT licence; the repository transfer micahflee/torbrowser-launcher → torproject/torbrowser-launcher was confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17 and recorded in leads.md L4.
assessment: Use it on Linux and, more importantly, make signature verification a trained habit for everyone regardless of platform — that is the transferable lesson. For your profile the operational points are: install from your distribution's package where possible, check that updates are actually arriving (a stalled launcher silently leaves an old browser in place), and pre-configure bridges for anyone working where Tor is blocked or monitored.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-05, latest release v0.3.7 (2024-01-28), tag v0.3.9, 890 stars, 89 open issues. Commits within the last two weeks but no release in nearly three years; a thin, stable wrapper now under Tor Project stewardship. Classified stable-low because the release gap is real for a security-adjacent tool.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Tor Browser itself is separately licensed (predominantly MPL-2.0 and BSD-family, as a Firefox derivative).
privacy: The launcher itself contacts the Tor Project to download and verify the browser, which is unremarkable, though on a monitored network that download is visible. Tor Browser then provides the anonymity properties.
alternatives: Direct download from torproject.org with manual GPG verification (required on Windows and macOS)
Tails, which bundles a verified Tor Browser in an amnesic environment
Orbot for routing Android traffic through Tor

name: Orbot
purpose: Android application that provides Tor connectivity for the device, either as a VPN-mode tunnel for selected applications or system-wide, with bridge support for censored networks.
journalism_use_case: Routing a reporter's phone traffic through Tor in a country where the network is monitored or specific services are blocked — including selectively tunnelling only the applications that matter, so a messaging app works while ordinary traffic looks normal.
pros: Per-application tunnelling is the practically important feature: routing everything through Tor is slow and conspicuous, while tunnelling just the messaging or browsing app is usable daily
Bridge support addresses the case that actually matters — networks where Tor itself is blocked — which is common in the jurisdictions exile media report on
Very actively maintained (release 17.9.8-RC-1 with Tor 0.4.9.17 on 2026-11-16; pushed the same day) by Guardian Project, which has a long record in this field
Repository transfer guardianproject/orbot → guardianproject/orbot-android verified by redirect, so the canonical path is current
cons: VPN-mode Tor on Android is visible to anyone inspecting the device, and in some jurisdictions the presence of Orbot is itself incriminating — a risk the app cannot mitigate
Tor over mobile networks is slow and battery-hungry, so users disable it exactly when they are travelling and most at risk
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION so the licence must be read from the repository, and the release/tag structure is confusing (RC releases against a v15-beta-2 tag)
Mobile Tor does not protect against application-level identifiers: an app that transmits an account identity over Tor is still identified
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,711 stars with 87 open issues, release 17.9.8-RC-1-tor-0.4.9.17 (2026-11-16) with same-day push, SPDX NOASSERTION; the repository is mirrored from Guardian Project's GitLab. Transfer confirmed by API redirect 2026-11-17.
assessment: Adopt for reporters working in censored or monitored networks, with per-app tunnelling rather than system-wide so it stays usable. For your profile the briefing that matters is twofold: configure bridges before travel rather than on arrival, and be clear that Tor hides the network path, not the account you log into — a journalist signing into an identified account over Tor has protected very little. In jurisdictions where Orbot's presence is itself risky, consider whether a clean device is the better answer.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 17.9.8-RC-1-tor-0.4.9.17 published the same day, 3,711 stars, 87 open issues. Same-day release and push, tracking current Tor versions, under a long-established maintainer.
licence: Not detected by the GitHub API — read the repository licence file (Guardian Project projects are predominantly BSD/GPL-family)
licence_restrictions: Unverified in this survey; confirm from the repository before redistribution.
costs: Free. No infrastructure. Cost is battery life and connection speed for the user.
privacy: Provides network-level anonymity for tunnelled applications, with bridges for censored networks. Residual risks: app presence is visible on the device, application-level identifiers defeat network anonymity, and mobile-network metadata (that the phone connected at all, and from which cell) is unaffected.
alternatives: Tor Browser for Android where only browsing needs protection
Outline or a trusted VPN where the goal is circumvention rather than anonymity
A clean, separately provisioned device for the highest-risk travel
blockers: Presence of the app may itself be incriminating in some jurisdictions

name: Outline
purpose: VPN system built on Shadowsocks that lets an organisation run its own servers and distribute access keys, with a manager application for creating servers and clients for all major platforms.
journalism_use_case: Giving reporters and sources in censored countries a circumvention channel the newsroom controls: you run the server, distribute keys to specific people, and revoke them individually — rather than relying on a commercial VPN whose infrastructure, logging and blocking status are outside your control.
pros: You control the infrastructure, which is the decisive difference from a commercial VPN: no third-party logs, no shared IP reputation, and keys you can revoke per person
Shadowsocks-based transport is designed to resist protocol-based blocking, so it survives in networks where standard VPN protocols are detected and dropped
Apache-2.0 with very active development (pushed 2026-11-17) and clients for all major platforms, so a mixed-device team is covered

Repository transfer Jigsaw-Code/outline-apps → OutlineFoundation/outline-apps verified by redirect — governance moved from Google's Jigsaw to an independent foundation, which is arguably an improvement for this use case
cons: Release metadata is badly stale (v1.10.1 from 2023-03-20 against a windows-v1.9.1 tag) despite current commits, so determining what version users should run takes effort — a real problem for security software
595 open issues across a multi-platform client suite
Running your own circumvention server makes you responsible for its operational security, and a server compromised by the adversary becomes a surveillance point on your most at-risk users
Circumvention is an arms race: your server's IP can be blocked, and maintaining access means rotating infrastructure, which is ongoing work rather than a one-time deployment
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 9,282 stars with 595 open issues, release v1.10.1 (2023-03-20) against current commits (pushed 2026-11-17), Apache-2.0; transfer from Jigsaw-Code to OutlineFoundation confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17. Outline's design for organisational circumvention is documented by the project.
assessment: Adopt it if you support people in censored networks — controlling your own circumvention infrastructure is materially better than recommending a commercial VPN. For your profile the realities to plan for: budget for IP rotation because servers get blocked, distribute keys through a channel that is itself protected, and treat the server as a high-value target since it sits in the path of your most exposed users' traffic. The stale release metadata is an irritant: pin and document the client versions you deploy.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release object v1.10.1 (2023-03-20), tag windows-v1.9.1, 9,282 stars, 595 open issues. Same-day commits with abandoned release tagging; activity is unambiguous but release hygiene is poor, which matters for a security tool.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure: a VPS per server (low single-digit monthly cost each, estimate) plus bandwidth, and — the real cost — periodic replacement of blocked servers. Budget for several servers and rotation rather than one.
privacy: You hold the infrastructure, so there is no third-party logging. The counterpart responsibility is that your server sees users' traffic destinations, making its security and your logging policy a source-protection question in their own right. Set logging to minimal deliberately.
alternatives: Tor with bridges where anonymity rather than access is the goal
Commercial VPNs for convenience, accepting third-party trust and shared blocking
Self-hosted WireGuard where protocol-based blocking is not the problem

name: ProofMode
purpose: Android application and library that attaches verifiable provenance to photos and videos at capture time — cryptographic hashes, signatures, and optional sensor and network metadata — producing a proof bundle alongside the media.
journalism_use_case: Strengthening the evidentiary value of material captured by reporters or trained citizen witnesses: a photo taken with ProofMode carries a signed hash and capture context, so its integrity from the moment of capture can be demonstrated rather than asserted — which matters when a government claims footage was fabricated.
pros: Provenance-at-capture is the strongest form of media verification, because it establishes integrity from origin rather than inferring manipulation afterwards — the same logic as C2PA but usable on an ordinary Android phone today
Designed for human-rights documentation by an organisation with a long track record in that field, so the threat model matches journalism rather than commercial content authentication
GPL-3.0 and actively maintained (3.5.1-BETA-3, 2026-11-13; pushed the same day), with a library form for embedding in a newsroom's own app
Optional metadata levels let the user decide how much context to attach, which matters because sensor and network metadata can identify the photographer
cons: Only helps for media captured with it, so it does nothing for the overwhelming majority of material that arrives already made — it is a programme to run with trained contributors, not a verification tool for incoming content

The metadata that makes proof strong (location, nearby networks, device identifiers) is exactly what can endanger the photographer, so the configuration is a direct trade-off between evidentiary value and source safety
Beta release line (3.5.1-BETA-3) and a modest community (266 stars, 21 open issues); the GitHub repository is a mirror of Guardian Project's GitLab
A signed hash proves the file has not changed since capture; it does not prove the scene was not staged, and that distinction will be lost on audiences unless carefully explained
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 266 stars with 21 open issues, release 3.5.1-BETA-3 (2026-11-13) with same-day push, GPL-3.0; the repository notes it is a mirror of the Guardian Project GitLab. The transfer guardianproject/proofmode → guardianproject/proofmode-android was confirmed by redirect in this session.
assessment: Pilot it where you work with trained contributors or stringers whose material may be challenged — that is the case where capture-time provenance pays off. For your profile the configuration decision is the whole story: attach enough to prove integrity, and think hard before enabling location and network metadata, because a proof bundle that identifies where the photographer stood can be the thing that endangers them. Pair it with C2PA signing at publication so the chain extends from capture to story.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release 3.5.1-BETA-3 published the same day, 266 stars, 21 open issues, GPL-3.0. Same-day release and push from an established maintainer; the beta designation reflects the release line rather than inactivity.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0: embedding the library in a distributed proprietary app triggers copyleft. Relevant if you build a newsroom contributor app around it.
costs: Free. No infrastructure unless you build a verification service around the proof bundles. Cost is contributor training and the storage of proof bundles alongside media.
privacy: Configurable, and the configuration is the privacy decision: full metadata strengthens proof and can identify the photographer, while minimal metadata is safer and weaker. Processing is local and nothing is uploaded by the app itself.
alternatives: c2pa-rs / c2patool for provenance signing at the publication rather than capture stage
Plain cryptographic hashing of captured files, published promptly, as a low-tech alternative
Standard camera capture plus careful chain-of-custody documentation
blockers: Proof-strengthening metadata can identify the photographer — configuration is a safety trade-off

name: Privacy Badger
purpose: Browser extension that learns to block third-party trackers by observing cross-site tracking behaviour rather than relying solely on blocklists, and removes outgoing link tracking and some fingerprinting vectors.
journalism_use_case: Reducing the trail a journalist leaves while researching: visiting a target's website, a procurement portal or an extremist forum would otherwise notify a dozen analytics and ad-tech companies, building a profile that associates your newsroom with the subjects you are investigating.
pros: Behavioural learning catches trackers that blocklists miss, which matters on the obscure regional and niche sites investigations actually visit — exactly where curated lists have gaps
Addresses a genuine and under-appreciated operational-security problem: research browsing builds a commercially held profile linking your organisation to your subjects
Maintained by EFF with a current release (release-2026.9.15, 2026-09-15; pushed 2026-11-12) and a clear institutional mission
Free, trivial to deploy across a newsroom, and requires no user discipline once installed
cons: Breaks some sites, and a journalist on deadline will disable it rather than diagnose it — so deployment needs a quick 'disable for this site' habit taught alongside it
Blocking trackers does not hide you from the site you are visiting, which still sees your IP and request — for that you need Tor or a separate egress, and users conflate the two
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION (EFF's licensing is GPL-family) so the licence needs reading for records
Behavioural learning means protection improves over time per profile, so a fresh browser profile starts weaker — relevant if reporters use disposable profiles for research
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,889 stars with 102 open issues, release release-2026.9.15 (2026-09-15), pushed 2026-11-12, SPDX NOASSERTION. EFF's maintenance and the behavioural-learning approach are documented by the project.
assessment: Adopt it newsroom-wide — it is free, requires nothing of users, and reduces a real exposure. For your profile the important framing is that it addresses third-party tracking, not visibility to the site itself: a reporter researching a surveillance vendor should use a separate browser profile and a non-newsroom egress as well, because the vendor's own server logs are the more consequential record. Teach the per-site disable so people do not switch it off globally.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, latest release release-2026.9.15 (2026-09-15), 3,889 stars, 102 open issues, SPDX NOASSERTION. Regular dated releases under EFF's institutional maintenance.
licence: GPL-family per EFF's licensing (GitHub reports NOASSERTION — read the repository licence file for records)
licence_restrictions: Unverified exactly in this survey; immaterial for use as a browser extension.
privacy: Blocks third-party tracking locally in the browser with no data sent to EFF. It does not conceal you from the visited site, which is the limitation to communicate clearly.
alternatives: uBlock Origin for broader blocklist-based blocking
Tor Browser where the visited site must not learn who you are
A dedicated research browser profile with a separate egress for sensitive targets
